paras: The Flomaton shooting of two Black railroad workers took place at Flomaton, Alabama, in August 1900, when two Black men were badly shot and taken to Montgomery for medical treatment. How they were wounded was never established in the coverage, which offered two competing reports, one describing a fight with tramps in a box car and the other a clash between white and Black men.

According to a Montgomery dispatch dated August 23, the two wounded men were brought to that city from Flomaton for treatment. The dispatch stated plainly that "just how the wounds were inflicted is not known." Neither the names of the wounded men nor the names of those who shot them were given.

In the first version, several Black "tramps" were found in an empty box car, resisted when ordered out, and a general fight followed in which several of them were wounded. The second version held that there had been "a clash between the whites and blacks at Flomaton" and that the two "railroad negroes" were shot. The dispatch did not favor either account, and it did not say who ordered the men out of the car or who fired.
No report of arrests, deaths, an inquest or charges appears in the coverage.

The shooting is known from a single brief wire item, printed on the front page of the Americus Times-Recorder in Georgia on August 24 under the headline "Two Negroes Shot." The item was written in a flat, uncommitted register, referring to the wounded men as "negroes" and "railroad negroes" and passing along both rumors without comment. No Alabama paper's account, follow-up story or Black-press report of the episode was found.
